title: The Very Democratic End of MAGA?
contentHtml:
(I’ve done my best to stay out of day-to-day politics — this is a walking newsletter prone to the philosophical and literary. Yet, politics does impact us all, especially its broad strokes, and so I cannot entirely ignore it. I’ll be back on the road in a week, and then back to more conventional postings.)

The first voter I heard praise Donald Trump was a mechanic in a forlorn town in upstate New York. It was days after Trump had descended the gold escalator, to the derision of the entire media, and I was only five hours into a drive across the United States to interview people about the American Dream.

A broken man in every way — his legs swollen from diabetes, his crumbling shop on a destitute main street — he was reticent to talk to me about anything other than my car, until I said, “One last thing, you don’t have to answer of course, but who you going to vote for president?” That got his attention, and he leaned against the shop wall, pulled out a smoke, took a drag, puffed up, and proclaimed, “Trump” with a certainty and pride that caught me off guard. “Trump?” I repeated, wanting to add, “That novelty candidate?”

But he was clear and sure here, no longer mumbling: “There’s no American dream for anyone who isn’t a lawyer or banker. Everyone else, we are getting a raw deal. Immigrants are taking all our jobs.”

By the end of that six-week trip through a taxonomy of American despair — the neighborhoods of the working class and the never worked, of physical banality surrounded by improbably sublime natural beauty — Trump’s name was a constant, and if his candidacy was a novelty, it was one selling like hotcakes.

He was what everyone wanted to talk about, either with lavish praise or diatribes of disdain. Unlike in the media, he wasn’t a punchline, but a force to be reckoned with, and the US would be reckoning with him for the next decade, and that meant the rest of the world as well.

Then on this Tuesday it all came to an end. Despite Trump’s pedantic admonition, he was on the ballot, as he’s been on every vote, op-ed, work of art, and academic panel of the last decade. And the voters were decisive, loud, and clear — we are done with this and done with this chaotic insurrection. Sure he’s still president for two years, and he’ll loom large until his death, but whatever magic he bottled up is all but used-up, and now he’s sliding into being just another run-of-the-mill politician doing what they all do in the end — engaged in a futile attempt to engineer his image fifty years from now.

That the end came via a fully fair and normal election and not via the fantasies of his opponents — via a military coup, dragged off in chains by cheering senators, or finally expiring on a throne of gold, poisoned by his subordinates, as the country wakes from a two decade darkness — speaks to a particular spell of his magic. The ability to warp his opponents into delusional hatred. He wasn’t a fascist intent on ending democracy, wasn’t the dark rider on the horse at the end of history, but rather just another charismatic politician making gilded promises to desperate voters that he couldn’t fulfill.

That first win in 2016, had he been the right sort of billionaire, had it been from the left, where the majority of the media and artists reside, it would have been celebrated as a just insurrection of the people. It would have gone down in their telling, as the voice of the common man overcoming evil forces of the powers that be. Songs and books would have been penned praising it, rather than condemning it.

It was an improbable win, culturally and mathematically. A renegade campaign waged in ways that they were not supposed to be waged. A coarse, garish, louche campaign that felt more like a late-night infomercial that broke containment, than a national presidential run. It was also, for those caught up in it, exceedingly exhilarating and just plain fun — a raucous party of misfits, of all shapes, incomes, religions, and races united in giving the middle finger to everyone who had ever laughed at them as stupid deplorables who didn’t know what was good for them.

To go from a staid rally for Jeb where the only emotion was a massive exclamation point, to a dour Cruz rally where darkness ruled, to a corporate Hillary rally where emotions were an entry in a spreadsheet to be measured out analytically, to a Trump event was like stumbling into that generous dive bar on the wrong side of town that smelled of vomit and perfume, where nobody cared who you were, how you looked, or what you thought, as long as you were a broken drunk like them. Welcome fellow loser, let’s get F-ed up!
